title: Twist as a Mechanical Switch for Reconfigurable Stacking in h-BN
authors: Gautham Vijayan, Zhaoheng Zhang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Michael Urbakh, Oded Hod, Xiang Gao, Elad Koren
abstract: Twistronics of layered materials has emerged as a highly active field due to its profound implications for quantum electronics and materials engineering. However, the controllable manipulation of interlayer stacking remains a significant experimental challenge. Here, the homogeneous contact between hexagonal boron nitride layers is shown to be reproducibly switched between two distinct stable stacking configurations via an externally applied torque. Combining experiments and computational modelling, we identify the stacking order of these stable states as the commensurate AA and AB modes. These two states are associated with different rotational torque maxima, exhibiting an asymmetry ratio of 0.7, and distinct dynamics as a function of the twist angle. Moreover, the peak torque values scale linearly with contact area, highlighting the dominant role of edge elasticity in the twisting process. Given that the AA and AB stacking modes correspond to different out-of-plane electric polarization states, our findings offer a pathway for reconfigurable nano- and micro-electromechanical devices.
summary: This work demonstrates that the stacking order of h-BN layers can be reversibly switched by applying external torque, a process termed 'twistronics.' By combining AFM experiments and atomistic simulations, the authors quantify the mechanical asymmetry between the stable AA and AB stacking states. This finding paves a pathway for designing reconfigurable nano-electromechanical devices based on controlled interlayer coupling.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of controllably switching the interlayer stacking configuration in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) using external mechanical torque.
main_result: The stacking can be reproducibly switched between AA and AB modes, exhibiting a measurable asymmetry ratio (approx. 0.7) and showing that the peak torque scales linearly with contact area, indicating dominant edge elasticity.
method: The study combines experimental measurements using an AFM setup to apply controlled torque with atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (LAMMPS) to model the atomic interactions.
model_or_system: The physical system is the contact interface between h-BN layers. The modeling involves simulating the torsional loading on these homojunctions, comparing flexible atomic reconstructions against more rigid theoretical models.
key_observables: Rotational torque (T) vs. angle ($	heta$), peak torque values, asymmetry ratio ($	ext{T}_{	ext{AB}} / 	ext{T}_{	ext{AA}'}$), and the scaling of torque with contact area ($	ext{T} \propto 	ext{A}$).
important_parameters: The key parameters are the stacking configurations (AA, AB), the applied external torque, and the contact area (A).
main_assumptions: The linear scaling of torque with area suggests that interfacial elasticity is the dominant mechanism governing the twisting process, overriding predictions from purely rigid models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanical setup, force-angle profiles showing torque peaks at specific angles ($60^\circ, 120^\circ$), and comparisons between experimental torque-angle profiles and MD simulation results, particularly regarding area scaling and yielding mechanisms.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the experimental measurement of torque switching in h-BN, then using atomistic simulations to reproduce and explain the observed asymmetry and the linear scaling of torque, contrasting ductile vs. brittle yielding mechanisms.
why_interesting: While focused on mechanics, the study of phase transitions (stacking changes) driven by external fields (torque) and the resulting polarization states offers analogies to controlling quantum states in engineered quantum materials.
